messages.author: 48ce750bd14fb4c8
messages.subject: myglmer2stan
parts:
I have a question:

In JAGS, burn-in shows on the screen and happens relatively quick (depending on data size& how long one sets burnin) however, mine appears to be 'silent' and, while set at 1000, taking forever, if it is running at all.

Is this common?

It has been sitting at Chain 1, Iteration: 1/10000 [ 0%] (Warmup)
For ~40 minutes. I've reset it a few times for lower burnin and interations to test this.

Thanks.


--
~Nik

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: myglmer2stan
parts:
On Thursday, November 3, 2016 at 12:32:41 PM UTC-4, Nik Ford wrote:
In JAGS, burn-in shows on the screen and happens relatively quick (depending on data size& how long one sets burnin) however, mine appears to be 'silent' and, while set at 1000, taking forever, if it is running at all.

It is running. You can set stan()'s refresh argument to be some number smaller than 10 to see updates at intervals more frequent than 10%. But it is quite likely that your model will take quite a long time and might still not produce good results without a reparameterization. You shouldn't need 10000 iterations anyway. I'm not sure what myglmer2stan is but you should probably be using stan_glmer in the rstanarm package.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] myglmer2stan
parts:
Did you start with fewer iterations first? One common difference between JAGS and Stan is that Stan often has much higher effective samples per iteration compared to JAGS. When I made the transition, I found I could often get more effective samples from Stan with 1/10 the iterations.

Second, I believe glmer2stan is depreciated and no longer maintained (last update was 2015). You should really look into the rstanarm package. 

Matt

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] myglmer2stan
parts:
Iterations are meaningless in and of themselves. What
you want to do is set a threshold for the effective
sample size (an estimate is reported as n_eff by Stan;
don't know about RStanArm). There can be orders of
magnitude or more differences in n_eff per iteration based
on algorithm. In some cases, Stan can generate an n_eff
in 500 iterations larger than JAGS can generate in 200,000
iterations, and in other cases, the n_eff rate per iterations
will be close to each other. It depends primarily on the
shape of the posterior.

Of course, I understand that by "my discipline" you may mean
reviewers won't accept a paper that doesn't have some
ridiculous number of draws in in it. Usually it's not much
use to get n_eff >> 100 or so, because at that point, the
mean estimates have 1/10 the error of the posterior standard
deviation.

- Bob

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] myglmer2stan
parts:
Yeah 100k is totally arbitrary and just nonsense without considering the particular MCMC algorithm. I wouldn't start with more than 2000 (the default) if you're using stan_glmer in rstanarm. If you need more you can increase but that's usually plenty for convergence (especially if you set the QR argument to TRUE).

Jonah

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] myglmer2stan
parts: Also for larger N data you often (not always) need _fewer_ iterations not more.

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] myglmer2stan
parts:
Forgot to say that instead of reparameterizing yourself I would first try stan_glmer. If you're still having trouble after that definitely follow up and we can help you write your own Stan program for your model.

Jonah
